passages.text: A model study for the classification of high-risk groups for cardiac arrest in general ward patients using simulation techniques

Currently, many hospitals use vital signs-based criteria such as modified early warning score (MEWS) and national early warning score (NEWS) to classify high-risk patients for cardiac arrest, but there are limitations in selecting high-risk patients with a possibility of cardiac arrest. The purpose of this study is to develop a cardiac arrest classification model to identify patients at high risk of cardiac arrest based on the patient family and past history, and blood test results after hospitalization, rather than vital signs. This study used electronic medical record (EMR) data from A university hospital, and patients in the high-risk group for cardiac arrest were defined as those who underwent cardio-pulmonary resuscitation (CPR) after cardiac arrest. Considering the use of the rapid response team of A university hospital, patients hospitalized in intensive care units (ICU), emergency medicine departments, psychiatric departments, pediatric departments, cardiology departments, and palliative care wards were excluded. This study included 325,534 patients, of which 3291 low-risk and 382 high-risk patients were selected for study. Data were split into training and validation data sets and univariate analysis was performed for 13 candidate risk factors. Then, multivariate analysis was performed using a bivariate logistic regression model, and an optimal model was selected using simulation analysis. In the training data set, it was calculated as sensitivity 75.25%, precision 21.59%, specificity 66.89%, accuracy 67.79%, F1 score 33.56, area under curve (AUC) 71.1 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 68.9–73.1 P value=<.001). In the validation data set, sensitivity 73.37%, precision 25.81%, specificity 75.03%, accuracy 74.86%, F1 score 38.19, AUC 74.2 (95% CI = 72.1–76.2, P value=<.001) were calculated. A model for classifying the high-risk group of cardiac arrest should be developed from various perspectives. In the future, in order to classify patients with high risk of cardiac arrest, a prospective study on the combined use of the model developed by this study and NEWS or MEWS should be conducted.
1. Introduction

According to “To Error is Human: Building a Safer Health Care System” by the Institute of Medicine (IOM) in 1999, 44,000 to 98,000 patients die annually in the United States due to medical errors, and these preventable adverse events This caused the country to lose 17 to 21 billion dollars. Since then, social interest in patient safety has increased, and patient safety has become a major framework for important health policies. According to a study by Wilson RM (1999), 4% to 17% of hospitalized patients reported that unexpected cardiac arrest or unplanned admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) occurred during hospitalization, and up to 70% of these unexpected situations could be prevented. In particular, as abnormal physical signs or changes in blood tests were observed in 60% to 84% of cardiorespiratory arrest patients 6-8 hours before onset, the importance of early detection and provision of interventional treatment when signs of deterioration have been emphasized.

For this reason, from May 2019, the Ministry of Health and Welfare of Korea and the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service implemented a rapid response system pilot project. The rapid response system of this pilot project is to form a separate rapid response team within the hospital to monitor the acute deterioration of inpatients in general wards and provide prompt treatment according to the high-risk patient classification system set in advance in the computer system. Through this, the mortality rate of inpatients was reduced, and treatment outcomes were improved.

One of the most important aspects of the rapid response team successful operation is a relatively accurate high-risk patient triage table. The rapid response team monitors the acute deterioration of inpatients in general wards according to the high-risk patient selection criteria set in the computer system. Currently, many hospitals use the Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS) and National Early Warning Score (NEWS) as criteria for selecting high-risk patients, but since these MEWS and NEWS select high-risk patients for cardiac arrest by vital signs, there are limitations in the work of selecting high-risk patients with potential cardiac arrest who have relatively stable vital signs. In order to overcome and solve this problem, a study was needed to select high-risk patients for cardiac arrest using other factors, including the patient family history and past history, in addition to vital signs.

Against this background, the authors conducted this study to analyze other factors, including family and past history, known as high-risk factors for cardiac arrest, in addition to vital signs, to establish a classification table for high-risk patients with cardiac arrest with high sensitivity and specificity.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Study design

This study is a retrospective study of medical records using the data recorded in the electronic medical record (EMR) of A university hospital. The protocol was approved by the institutional review board of Daegu Catholic Medical Center (approval number: CR-23-028-L).
2.2. Study subjects

A university hospital has been using EMR since 2013, so the data of patients admitted to general wards from January 2013 to December 2021 were used in this study. High-risk patients were defined as patients with cardiac arrest, but data on whether cardiac arrest occurred did not exist in the EMR because it was the condition of the patient. However, since cardio-pulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is performed when cardiac arrest occurs, high-risk patients were defined as those who performed CPR to extract data from EMR. In addition, since the high-risk patient selection will be used by the rapid response team of A university hospital, the scope of data collection was set to the general ward within the scope of the rapid response team. That is, the data of patients admitted to the ICU, emergency medicine ward, psychiatric ward, pediatric ward, cardiology ward, and hospice ward were excluded. In addition, patients who signed an agreement to give up resuscitation were excluded from this study because they did not perform CPR even if cardiac arrest occurred.
2.3. Measurements and variables

In this study, the response (dependent) variable was dichotomous data, either high-risk patients or non-high-risk patients. That is, “cardiac arrest occurred or did not occur” and “CPR was performed or not performed” to extract data from EMR. For information on whether or not CPR was performed, the health insurance treatment benefit standard codes M5873, M5874, M5875, M5876, and M5877 were used.

Main risk factors and additional risk factors were considered as explanatory (independent) variables. Smoking, high body mass index (BMI), hypertension, diabetes, high blood cholesterol, and family history of coronary artery disease were considered as major risk factors for cardiac arrest. Additional risk factors for cardiac arrest include older age, male sex, use of illicit drugs (cocaine, amphetamines), low potassium, low magnesium, low glomerular filtration rate (GFR), low creatinine, family history of coronary artery disease, history of cardiac arrest, family history of cardiac arrest, history of heart disease, family history of heart disease, sleep disorder, and major operation were considered. A GFR value of 90 or higher was defined as normal, 60 to 89 mild, 30 to 59 moderate, 15 to 29 severe, and <15 failures.
2.4. Statistical analysis and modeling

Summary for characteristics and outcomes were performed using descriptive analysis, the values of mean ± standard deviation presented for continuous variables and the values of frequency(percent) for categorical variables. Differences between high-risk and non-high-risk patients were analyzed for the main risk factors and additional risk factors for cardiac arrest. Machine learning methods used in the medical field for classification of binary data include random forest, boosting machine, decision tree, and eXGBoosting machine, support vector machine, and logistic regression, etc. Among them, in this study, logistic regression was used, which can easily explain between risk factors and dependent variables. First, each univariate analysis was performed, and risk factors satisfying P value < .05 were selected as explanatory variables for performing binary logistic multiple regression analysis to develop the final model. In univariate analysis, a 2-sample t-test was performed for quantitative data and a chi-square test was performed for qualitative data. The entire data set generates a random number between 0 and 1 for each data, divides the entire data set 1: 1 based on 0.5, develops a high-risk patient selection model as a training data set, and tests the developed model as a validation data set performed. Using the validation data set, model evaluation measures such as sensitivity, specificity, precision, accuracy, F1 score, and area under curve (AUC) were calculated using the values predicted by the developed high-risk patient screening model and the values of actual data, and an receiver operating characteristic (ROC) figure was created. In order to find the optimal model, the following process was performed to find the optimal combination of the K risk factors selected in the univariate analysis, and among them (c) and (d) were repeatedly simulated several times. The simulation was performed a total of 2K-1 times, starting with a model with only 1 risk factor selected in univariate analysis as an explanatory variable, then 2 combinations, 3 combinations, and so on, and finally K combinations. In this study, the optimal model means the model that yields the highest sensitivity and specificity values calculated in the training data set and validation data set, respectively.

The explanatory variables included in the final high-risk selection model were evaluated for multicollinearity, and the Hosmer–Lemeshow test was performed to test the goodness of fit of the developed model. All tests were 2-sided and a P value of <.05 considered to indicate statistical significance and SAS software version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC) was used to analysis.
3. Result
3.1. Patient characteristics

The total number of study subjects was 325,534, with 352,152 low-risk patients and 382 high-risk patients. In order to set the number of study subjects between the 2 groups as 1:10, 3291 subjects were selected through 1% sampling in the low-risk patient group. In order to set the training data set and the validation data set to be 1:1, a uniform (0,1) random number was used in each of the low-risk and high-risk groups and divided 1:1. Finally, 1832 people were selected for the training data set and 1738 people were selected for the validation data set. The process of setting the training data set and validation data set from the total number of patients is shown in Figure 1.
The process of setting the training data set and validation data set from the total number of patients.
3.2. Univariate analysis

Table 1 shows the results of univariate analysis comparing the low-risk group and the high-risk group for risk factor candidate variables in the training data set. Age was 50.79 ± 24.79 in the low-risk group and 62.13 ± 15.53 in the high-risk group, and there was a statistically significant difference between the 2 groups (P value = .001). By gender, 749 males (45.8%) in the low-risk group and 130 (65.78%) in the high-risk group showed a statistically significant difference between the 2 groups (P value < .001). In addition, among the candidate risk factors, a total of 13 risk factors such as age, sex, BMI, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, family history of myocardial infarction, family history of cardiac arrest, past history of heart disease, sleep disorder, total cholesterol, creatinine and GFR showed statistically significant differences between the low-risk group and the high-risk group.

3.3. Simulation and multivariate analysis

As described in the statistical analysis method, a total of 13 significant risk factors were used in the univariate analysis, and multivariate analysis was performed using a bivariate logistic regression model as a machine learning method. In order to find the optimal model with the highest sensitivity and specificity, 213-1 = 8191 combinations, which is the number of all combinations that can be created with 13 risk factors, were analyzed by simulation. Among them, the model selected as the most optimal model was a combination of 9 risk factors, and the results are shown in Table 2. Seven risk factors were selected as smoking (Yes), Sex (Male), hypertension (Yes), diabetes (Yes), past history of heart disease (Yes), age (≥65), sleep disorder (Yes), total cholesterol (≤160) and creatinine. The purpose of this study is to develop a model for screening patients with high risk of cardiac arrest. Therefore, we did not consider whether each risk factor was individually statistically significant or not in the results of multivariate analysis, but focused on developing a model that well selects patients with high risk of cardiac arrest. According to the results of multivariate analysis, patients who smoked had an odds ratio of 1.02 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.54–1.95) to be at high risk of cardiac arrest compared to patients who did not smoke. Male patients had an OR of 2.99 (95% CI: 1.83–4.90) at high risk of cardiac arrest compared to female patients. The odds ratio for patient with hypertension was 1.01 (95% CI: 0.55–1.84). Patients with diabetes had 1.20 (95% CI: 0.58–2.48) probability of having a higher risk of cardiac arrest. The odds ratio for patients with a history of heart disease was 1.64 (95% CI: 0.65–4.11). Patients aged ≥ 65 years had 2.26 (95% CI: 0.40–12.71) probability of having a higher risk of cardiac arrest. The odds ratio for patients with a sleep disorder was 2.33 (95% CI: 0.66–8.19), patients with the total cholesterol below 160mg/dl was 2.83 (95% CI: 1.58–5.05). The odds ratio of having a high risk of cardiac arrest was 1.44 (95% CI: 1.08–1.91) when creatinine was 1 mg/dl higher. The fitness of the model was evaluated using the Hosmer–Lemeshow test, and multicollinearity between risk factors was not detected.

3.4. Cardiac arrest classification model

Based on the results of multivariate analysis, the model for classifying patients with high risk of cardiac arrest is as follows. Cardiac arrest risk score (CARS) were first calculated to classify patients with high risk of cardiac arrest. CARS can be calculated using regression coefficients of multivariate analysis results. Cardiac arrest risk classification model (CACM) was defined using the CARS. If the CARS was 50 or more, it was classified as a high-risk group for cardiac arrest, and conversely, if the CARS was <50, it was classified as a low-risk group for cardiac arrest. 3.5. Model evaluation

The CACM developed using the training data set was evaluated in various ways. The predicted values of the low-risk and low-risk groups for cardiac arrest were calculated by inputting the values of the risk factors in the training data set and the validation data set into the developed model. This was compared with the data values of the actual cardiac arrest low-risk and high-risk groups to calculate model evaluation measure values. As the model evaluation measure values, sensitivity, specificity, precision, accuracy, F1 score, and AUC were calculated and are shown in Table 3. In the training data set, it was calculated as sensitivity 75.25%, precision 21.59%, specificity 66.89%, accuracy 67.79%, F1 score 33.56, AUC 71.1 (95% CI = 68.9–73.1 P value=<.001). In the validation data set, sensitivity 73.37%, precision 25.81%, specificity 75.03%, accuracy 74.86%, F1 score 38.19, AUC 74.2 (95% CI = 72.1–76.2, P value=<.001) were calculated. In addition, ROC figures were drawn in the training data set and the validation data set, respectively, using the low-risk and high-risk group data calculated using the CACM and the actual data (Fig. 2).

4. Discussion

The important points that the authors found in this study are as follows. First, a total of 13 single factors (age, sex, BMI, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, family history of myocardial infarction, family history of cardiac arrest) were found among the factors including the patient past history, family history, and blood tests, excluding vital sign, past history of heart disease, sleep disorder, total cholesterol, creatinine and GFR) was found to be a single factor associated with the risk group for cardiac arrest. Second, we found a model that can predict the risk group of cardiac arrest with the highest sensitivity and specificity using a machine learning method with 13 factors. This model consists of 9 factors out of 13 single factors, each factor being smoking (Yes), sex (Male), hypertension (Yes), diabetes (Yes), past history of heart disease (Yes), age (≥65), sleep disorder (Yes), total cholesterol (≤160) and creatinine.

Smoking has already been shown to be associated with sudden cardiac death in many studies. In particular, according to Aune meta-analysis study, the possibility of sudden cardiac death was statistically significantly higher in patients with a history of smoking than in the control group. In a meta-analysis study by Pan, it was known that patients with a history of hypertension and heart disease had a higher possibility of sudden cardiac death than the control group. Additionally, sleep disorder is also known to be a risk factor for sudden cardiac death, and Blackwell suggested that increased arrhythmogenicity due to sleep disorder could cause sudden cardiac arrest.

Increased creatinine eventually means problems with kidney function, and many studies have already reported that patients with reduced kidney function have a higher incidence of sudden cardiac death than the control group. In this study, a model was created by dividing the cholesterol level into 160 mg/dL standard. It is known through many studies that high cholesterol levels are generally associated with sudden cardiac death. However, as a result of our study, the cardiac arrest patient group showed a statistically significantly lower cholesterol level than the control group, and the average value was 145.14 ± 58.4 mg/dL, which was a low value. Many studies have reported that patients with low cholesterol are more likely to develop cardiac arrest than controls. In particular, in Yang study, the adjusted OR for cardiac arrest was 6.53 when the cholesterol level was <148 mg/dL. Referring to these results, the present authors created a predictive model by dividing the cholesterol level by the standard of 160 mg/dL to clarify the risk of low cholesterol level.

Algorithm-based studies to predict cardiac arrest in hospitalized patients have already been conducted. In Kwon case, an algorithm was created using 4 vital signs (systolic blood, HR, respiratory rate, and body temperature), and most studies were conducted with studies including vital signs. Hyouk Jae Lim et al (2022) utilized the Korean Cardiac Arrest Research Consortium database to calculate pH, lactate, age, shockable rhythm, prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) factors for the calculation of the ED-PLANN score for screening cardiac arrest. In addition, with the development of artificial intelligence technology, studies on models or systems for high-risk patient selection have been conducted using various deep learning methods. Yunseob Shin et al (2022) proposed a pDEWS model to screen for cardiac arrest using age and 20 consecutive vital signs, namely respiratory rate, heart rate, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and body temperature. Qinhua Tang et al (2022) utilized a temporal convolutional network (TCN) based on the structure of a convolutional network to capture medical information from an electronic health records (EHR) sequence through higher parallelism, thereby improving the performance of cardiac arrest prediction.

On the other hand, since models for selecting high-risk patients are developed retrospectively using patient data, the models change when the data change. The accuracy of the high-risk patient screening model can be reduced if a single model is developed and used in different hospitals. Since the high-risk patient selection model is used by each hospital, the model should be developed using the hospital data. Through this, the results of selecting high-risk patients based on the model can increase the concordance of the actual patient condition.

Unlike previous studies, this study did not include the patient real-time vital sign, and an algorithm was created using the patient history, age, gender, creatinine level, and cholesterol level. The purpose of this study was to develop the developed algorithm to be used in combination with MEWS and NEWS, rather than used alone. In the case of MEWS and NEWS, all factors change in real time are the patient vital signs. Signs that change in real time can indicate the patient rapidly changing condition, but if there is an algorithm that can estimate the patient risk factors immediately after hospitalization, it is thought that it can help medical staff select high-risk patients right after hospitalization. In the end, a prospective study on the combined use of the algorithm developed by this study and NEWS or MEWS should be conducted in the future.

The limitations of this study are as follows. Since this study was conducted only for patients from a single center, there are limitations in presenting the results of this study in general. As a result of analysis with the existing data results, a prospective study on this result should be conducted in the future. This study targeted only the patient groups to which the rapid response team responded, excluding the ICU, emergency medicine ward, and cardiology ward, which may have a high risk of cardiac arrest.
5. Conclusion

In order to prevent unexpected cardiac arrest in hospitalized patients, a high-risk group for cardiac arrest is classified and a rapid response team is operated. A model for classifying the high-risk group of cardiac arrest should be developed from various perspectives. In this study, a model was developed to classify the high-risk group for cardiac arrest using the patient family history, past history, and blood test results after hospitalization. In the future, in order to classify patients with high risk of cardiac arrest, a prospective study on the combined use of the model developed by this study and NEWS or MEWS should be conducted.
